title: Spot the Added Letter
statement:
You get two strings of lowercase letters, s and t. To make t, someone took every letter of s, added exactly one more lowercase letter, and shuffled the result.

Return the letter that was added. The added letter may be one that already appears in s.

examples.why: Both strings have one l, two o and one p. The s is the only letter left over.
Every letter of t also appears in s, so checking "which letter of t is missing from s" finds nothing. Counting does: t has three a, s has two.
With an empty s, the whole of t is the added letter.

constraints: s and t contain only lowercase English letters
hints: The two strings differ by a single letter. What stays the same when you shuffle a string?
The count of each letter does not change under shuffling. Count the letters of t and subtract the letters of s; one count is left at 1.
You can do it without a table: XOR all character codes of both strings together. Every letter of s cancels its copy in t, and only the added letter remains.

explain.intuition:
Shuffling moves letters around but never changes how many of each there are. So the added letter is the one whose count in t is one higher than in s. A 26-slot count array finds it in one pass over each string.

XOR gives the same answer with no table at all. x ^ x = 0 and XOR does not care about order, so if you XOR every character code of s and t together, every letter that appears in both cancels out in pairs. What is left is the code of the extra letter. Summing the codes and subtracting works for the same reason.
steps: XOR acc with the character code of every letter in s.
XOR acc with the character code of every letter in t.
Every paired letter has cancelled. Return the letter whose code is acc.
pitfalls: Looking for a letter of t that does not occur in s. The added letter can be a duplicate of one already there, like in "aab" → "abaa".
Comparing the strings position by position. They are shuffled, so positions mean nothing.
Sorting both strings works but costs O(n log n) for a problem that needs one linear pass.

solutions.title: Sort both and compare
solutions.idea: After sorting, the strings match position by position until the first place where t has the extra letter.

solutions.title: Letter counts
solutions.idea: Count letters in t, subtract the letters in s. The letter left with count 1 is the added one.

solutions.title: XOR of all codes
solutions.idea: Letters present in both strings cancel in pairs under XOR, leaving only the added one.

followups: t now has k extra letters instead of one. Which of the three approaches still works, and what does it return?
The strings can contain any Unicode text. What changes in the counting version and in the XOR version?
